sources.quote: From 手(て) (te, “hand”) + の (no, “-'s”, genitive particle) + 平(ひら) (hira, “flat”). Compare English flat of one's hand.

headline: Tōtobu is 尊 (tōto, the stem of 尊い (tōtoi, “noble, exalted, sacred”)) plus ぶ (-bu, “to act like”).

sources.quote: 尊 (tōto, tatto, stem of 尊い (tōtoi, tattoi, “noble, exalted, sacred”)) + ぶ (-bu, “to act like”)

The ぶ (-bu) suffix usually conjugated with the upper bigrade pattern (上二段活用 (kami nidan katsuyō)), and 尊ぶ conjugated this way in Old Japanese. Since the Heian period, 尊ぶ shifted to conjugate using the classical yodan pattern, the precursor to the modern godan conjugation (五段活用 (godan katsuyō)).

headline: Kuki is from Old Japanese, attested in the Kakyō Hyōshiki of 772 with the phonetic spelling 倶基.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, attested in the Kakyō Hyōshiki of 772 with the phonetic spelling 倶基. In turn, from Proto-Japonic *kukuy.
This word has an alternating form くく (kuku) which only occurs in compounds. For the reason of this vowel alternation, see WT:AJPX#Standalone forms and combining forms.

headline: Asa is from Old Japanese and is likely cognate with a Korean word for hemp.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese.
Likely cognate with Korean 삼 (sam, “hemp”).

headline: Kaerimiru is 帰り (kaeri, the stem of 帰る (kaeru, “to return, to go home”)) plus 見る (miru, “to look, to watch, to take care”).

sources.quote: From 帰(かえ)り (kaeri, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 帰(かえ)る (kaeru, “to return, to go home”).) + 見(み)る (miru, “to look, to watch, to take care”).
The み (mi) is written as an okurigana to indicate the reading of 顧.

headline: Teibō is from the Middle Chinese compound 堤防, literally “dike, embankment + dike”.

sources.quote: /teibau/ → /teibɔː/ → /teiboː/
From Middle Chinese compound 堤防 (dei? bjang, literally “dike, embankment + dike”). Compare modern Cantonese reading tai⁴ fong⁴.

examples.ja: 水は堤防を越えた。
examples.en: The water ran over the banks.

examples.ja: 堤防が洪水を防いだ。
examples.en: The levee kept the floodwater back.

headline: Minamoto is derived from 水 (mi, “water”), な (na, Old Japanese possessive particle) and 元 (moto, “origin, source”).

sources.quote: Derived from 水 (mi, “water”, combining form); な (na, Old Japanese possessive particle); 元, 本 (moto, “origin, source”).

Vovin believes that the na in the initial mina- element is not a genitive particle, but rather actually meant "water", contending that the mi was instead the honorific prefix 御 (mi-). See also 港 (minato, “sluice; port”).

examples.ja: その川の源は日本アルプス山中にある。
examples.en: The river has its origin in the Japan Alps.
furigana: は日本アルプス山中にある。

examples.ja: この川は長野の山々に源を発している。
examples.en: This river rises in the mountains in Nagano.

headline: Tomonau is from classical 伴ふ (tomonafu), formed from とも (tomo, “companion”) plus なふ (nafu, verb-forming suffix).

sources.quote: From classical yodan(四段活用) verb 伴(ともな)ふ (tomonafu), formed from とも (tomo, “companion”) + なふ (nafu, verb-forming suffix).

examples.ja: 豪雨は雷を伴った。
examples.en: The heavy rain was accompanied with thunder.

examples.ja: 権力には責任が伴う。
examples.en: Power carries responsibility with it.
